summary: GrowWhere is a map-based prototype that helps farmers explore what to grow and compare where to grow it using NASA weather data and USDA soil and cropland information. Users draw a field or search an area, choose one of seven crops, and set an irrigation scenario. The map displays historical suitability and explicit No data zones, alongside annual cost and harvest-price context. Users can compare two fields and download a PDF containing the calculation formulas, available inputs, source versions, and limitations. Prepared map products make exploration responsive without recalculating every map movement. The current scored pilot covers Kansas; the interface supports North American navigation. GrowWhere makes agricultural data easier to examine while clearly distinguishing research screening from validated planting or irrigation advice.
details:
GrowWhere is a map-based agricultural decision-support prototype developed by RightVersion for the NASA Space Apps Challenge task “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.” It brings weather, soil and agricultural information into one accessible interface, helping farmers explore crop choices and compare growing conditions across locations.

Users start by drawing their field boundary or choosing to search for suitable areas. They then select a crop and specify their growing area and irrigation assumptions. The prototype supports seven crop profiles: spring wheat, soybeans, corn, sorghum, spring barley, oats and cotton. Colored map zones communicate suitability, while areas without sufficient critical inputs explicitly display “No data.” Large controls and a guided workflow make the interface approachable for people with limited experience using digital tools.

The analysis combines historical daily weather from NASA POWER with soil properties from USDA SSURGO and land-cover information from the USDA Cropland Data Layer. Its experimental suitability index considers seven factors: temperature, water availability, soil acidity, available water capacity, drainage, slope and texture. The calculation uses explicit weights and a rule that limits the final score when a critical factor is extremely unfavorable. FAO-56 evapotranspiration equations and crop coefficients support the seasonal water-balance calculation.

GrowWhere also displays annual USDA ERS production costs and historical harvest prices. This gives users economic context alongside environmental suitability. These figures do not establish current market demand or guarantee profitability.

To support responsive map exploration, the system calculates suitability products ahead of time and stores versioned results in SQLite with spatial indexes. The browser retrieves prepared values for the selected scenario instead of recalculating the analysis for every map movement. Adjacent zones of the same suitability class join visually while missing-data gaps remain visible.

Users can save one field and explore a second, then compare their suitability scores, individual factors and seasonal water balance. The comparison identifies differences between scenarios rather than presenting incompatible results as a fair ranking. Downloadable PDF reports document the selected conditions, calculation equations, available numerical inputs, source versions and limitations. They distinguish point calculations from overview averages and field aggregation.

The application uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the interface, a Python API, SQLite/RTree for prepared map storage and Matplotlib for analytical PDF reports. Optional NASA GIBS layers provide MODIS vegetation and SMAP soil-moisture imagery separately from the numerical index. NOAA NWS forecasts and selected K-State references support a separate planning-readiness check.

The current numerical pilot covers Kansas using the 2025 historical season. Users can navigate North America, but territories without prepared inputs remain “No data.” The method still requires field calibration, and coarse climate information limits interpretation at individual-field scale. Verified sowing dates and recommended irrigation volumes are not yet available.

GrowWhere’s intended contribution is to make agricultural evidence easier to understand, compare and discuss with local agronomists. Future development includes broader validated coverage, finer prepared layers, automated refresh jobs and integration of field measurements.
